headline: Splitting the Tabs primitives into an imported module changes almost nothing for anyone: the compile-time boundary was already crossed inside the single-file version.

microbench.why: `vanilla-solid` at 186,000 renders/s and `vanilla` at 157,000 lead, with `next-yak-css` at 139,000 — down 13% from the single-file case, the only lane where the boundary is clearly visible, since a css prop can no longer resolve a fragment declared elsewhere. `next-yak` at 81,000 is unchanged: its per-tab wrapper survives either way. `yak-solid` at 10,000 is likewise near-unchanged, still paying a Solid component per tab.

autocannon.why: `vanilla` at 723 req/s and `vanilla-solid` at 685 lead, `next-yak-css` at 652 close behind. `yak-solid` at 70 req/s and `panda-props` at 89 are the lanes whose per-element work lands inside the request.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

attribution.why: `vanilla-solid` at 1.11 ms leads, then `next-yak-css` at 1.44 ms and `stylex` at 1.49 ms, all with empty lib buckets. `next-yak` at 3.74 ms books 1.59 ms of lib — more than double its single-file figure of 0.739 ms, which is the module boundary priced exactly. `yak-solid` at 16.0 ms books 1.17 ms of its own and leaves 13.1 ms in the framework, the per-tab component again rather than a boundary effect.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

hydrate.why: `vanilla-solid` at 40.9 ms leads, then `stylex` at 47.6 ms and `vanilla` at 47.8 ms. `yak-solid` at 115 ms and `goober` at 193 ms are the only lanes that separate upward.

inp.why: `cn` at 6.4 ms and `next-yak-css-nofold` at 6.7 ms lead; most lanes answer between 7 and 9 ms. The Solid lanes' 18.5 ms and 80.6 ms come from their bump changing the tab count and rebuilding the list, which the React pass does not do. `emotion` at 27.7 ms and `panda-props` at 25.1 ms are genuine.

mount.why: `vanilla-solid` mounts in 30.6 ms, three times faster than the React field's 90.7 ms floor, by cloning templates instead of building a fiber tree. `yak-solid` at 102 ms spends that advantage on per-tab components.

renderTiming.why: One style recalculation per lane near 0.87 ms, identical to the single-file case. Where the declarations were authored has no effect on what the style engine matches.

payload.why: Byte-for-byte the single-file case: `vanilla` at 2,690 gz B, the next-yak css-prop lanes at roughly 2,700 B, `yak-solid` at 8,307 B and `cn` at 23,474 B. The split changes which module a declaration lives in, never what ships.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

nsweep.why: `vanilla-solid` at 23.9 ms and `vanilla` at 29.9 ms hold the flattest lines at the largest size, `next-yak` reaches 70.3 ms and `yak-solid` 404 ms — the same ordering as the single-file case, with the same causes.

crossCase: The Example `tabs` with the primitives moved to `parts.tsx`. `next-yak` moves 82,500 to 81,000 renders/s, `next-yak-css` 160,000 to 139,000 and `yak-solid` 11,100 to 10,000 — every gap is small, because `styled(TabInternal)` already denied both compilers the fold in the single-file case. The module boundary is real but this component had spent its folding budget before reaching it.
